title: Vyvanse and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and the Vyvanse Hangover
excerpt: Can you drink on Vyvanse? How the stimulant masks how drunk you are, strains your heart, how long it lasts, why the Vyvanse hangover feels so bad, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Vyvanse? How it masks how drunk you feel, strains your heart, how long to wait, why the Vyvanse hangover hits hard, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Vyvanse and alcohol don't react with each other in a dramatic chemical way, but mixing them is still a bad idea, and most prescribers will tell you to avoid it or keep it very light. The main problem is that Vyvanse is a stimulant. It makes you feel more alert and in control than your blood alcohol level says you are, so it's easy to drink more than you meant to. Both substances also push on your heart, both dry you out, and Vyvanse lasts a long time, which means an evening drink often lands while the medication is still fully active. The morning after tends to be rough: poor sleep, low mood, and a heavier hangover than the same drinks would normally cause. This guide explains what is actually going on in your body, how long the medication lasts, what the "Vyvanse hangover" is, and the warning signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Talk to your prescriber before you combine the two, even occasionally. If you do drink, keep it to one or two drinks, count them deliberately instead of going by how you feel, eat a real meal first (Vyvanse kills appetite), and drink water alongside. Never take an extra dose of Vyvanse to "sober up" or push through a night out, and never skip or double doses around drinking without asking your doctor. If you notice chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, fainting, confusion, or a seizure, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and dose. **Talk to your prescriber before mixing Vyvanse with alcohol**, especially if you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, or a history of seizures, or if you take other medicines such as antidepressants. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room if** you or someone else has chest pain, a pounding or irregular heartbeat that doesn't calm down with rest, trouble breathing, fainting, severe confusion or agitation, a very high body temperature, or a seizure.

## What Vyvanse Is and How It Works

Vyvanse is the brand name for **lisdexamfetamine**. It's prescribed for ADHD in adults and children over 6, and in the US it's also approved for moderate to severe binge eating disorder in adults. It belongs to the amphetamine family, the same broad group as Adderall.

What makes Vyvanse different is that it's a **prodrug**. The capsule or chewable tablet you swallow is not active on its own. After it's absorbed, enzymes mostly in your red blood cells slowly snip off a piece of the molecule and release **dextroamphetamine**, the part that actually does the work. Because that conversion happens gradually, Vyvanse has a smoother start, a long steady effect, and a gentler tail than many immediate-release stimulants.

Once active, dextroamphetamine raises the levels of two brain chemicals, **dopamine and norepinephrine**. That improves focus and impulse control in people with ADHD. It also does several things throughout the body:

- Raises heart rate and blood pressure
- Reduces appetite, often a lot
- Makes it harder to fall asleep
- Can increase anxiety or jitteriness in some people

Keep those four effects in mind. Each one gets worse, or more risky, when you add alcohol.

### How long Vyvanse lasts

For most people, the effects of a morning dose last roughly 10 to 14 hours. The drug's prescribing information describes effects in clinical studies lasting into the evening for many adults. That matters for drinking. If you take your dose at 8 a.m., the medication can still be noticeably active at 7 or 8 p.m., right when most people have their first drink. Unlike a short-acting pill that has mostly worn off by dinner, Vyvanse is often still in the game.

## Why Vyvanse and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Real Mechanisms

There are four main ways the two clash. None involves alcohol "breaking" the capsule or a toxic chemical reaction. The problems come from how two drugs with opposite effects push and pull on the same body.

### 1. The masking effect: you feel less drunk than you are

This is the biggest practical danger. Alcohol is a depressant. It makes you sleepy, slows your reactions, and eventually tells you to stop. Vyvanse is a stimulant that keeps you alert and awake. When both are in your system, the stimulant can cover up many of the signals your body normally uses to tell you you've had enough.

The key point is that **masking hides the feeling of being drunk, not the alcohol itself.** Your blood alcohol level is exactly what it would be without Vyvanse. Your judgment, coordination, and reaction time are still impaired. You just notice it less. Studies of stimulants combined with alcohol, including research on caffeinated alcoholic drinks and on prescription stimulants, have consistently found that people feel less impaired while their actual performance is still affected.

That gap leads to the most common bad outcomes:

- **Drinking much more than usual**, because the "I'm done" signal doesn't arrive on time.
- **Driving or making risky decisions** because you feel sharp.
- **Alcohol poisoning**, because you can keep going past the point where you'd normally have gotten sleepy and stopped.

The masking is also uneven. As the Vyvanse wears off late in the evening, the alcohol doesn't. People sometimes describe suddenly feeling very drunk all at once near the end of the night. That's the stimulant cover lifting while the alcohol is still there.

### 2. Strain on your heart

Vyvanse raises your heart rate and blood pressure. Alcohol has its own effects on the heart: in the short term it can speed up the heart rate, and heavy drinking in one session is linked to heart rhythm problems. Doctors sometimes call that pattern "holiday heart," where a binge triggers an irregular rhythm such as atrial fibrillation in someone who otherwise seems healthy.

Put the two together and your heart is being pushed from two directions. For a healthy young adult on a normal dose who has one drink, this is unlikely to cause a crisis. But the risk climbs with heavier drinking, higher doses, dehydration, poor sleep, and any underlying heart problem, including ones you may not know about. The Vyvanse label carries warnings about serious heart events in people with existing heart disease and tells doctors to check heart history before prescribing.

If you've ever felt your heart pound after drinking, our guide to [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains the usual causes. On Vyvanse, that same feeling deserves more caution, not less.

### 3. Dehydration and an empty stomach

Vyvanse suppresses appetite. Many people on it barely eat during the day. Alcohol on an empty stomach gets absorbed faster, so your blood alcohol rises more quickly and peaks higher than it would after a meal.

Alcohol also makes you urinate more, and stimulants can raise body temperature and make you sweat, especially if you're dancing or in a hot room. So the combination tends to leave you dehydrated, under-fed, and with a faster-rising blood alcohol level. That's a recipe for feeling terrible the next day and for getting drunk faster than you expected that night.

### 4. Mood, anxiety, and sleep

Both drugs affect brain chemistry in ways that can swing your mood:

- **Anxiety:** Stimulants can make some people jittery or anxious. Alcohol relieves anxiety for a few hours and then rebounds, often leaving you more anxious the next day. Stacking the two can make that rebound sharper.
- **Sleep:** Vyvanse makes it harder to fall asleep. Alcohol makes you drowsy at first but breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night. Together, they can wreck a night's rest.
- **Low mood:** Coming down from a stimulant can bring a dip in mood and energy. Alcohol is a depressant and tends to deepen that dip.

If you have depression, bipolar disorder, or an anxiety disorder, this is a much bigger deal, and it's worth a direct conversation with your prescriber.

## The "Vyvanse Hangover": Why the Next Day Feels So Bad

A lot of people search for "Vyvanse hangover" because the morning after drinking on Vyvanse feels worse than a normal hangover. That's not your imagination. Several things stack up:

- **You probably drank more than you thought.** The masking effect means more alcohol, which means a bigger hangover.
- **You likely slept badly.** Stimulant still active at bedtime plus alcohol-fragmented sleep equals very little real rest. Poor sleep makes every hangover symptom worse.
- **You were dehydrated and under-fed.** Low appetite all day, alcohol on an empty stomach, extra fluid loss.
- **The stimulant comedown.** As Vyvanse wears off, some people feel tired, flat, irritable, or low. That's sometimes called a crash or rebound. Adding alcohol's own next-day mood dip makes it heavier.

The result is often a mix of exhaustion, headache, brain fog, low mood, and anxiety that can feel out of proportion to how much you remember drinking.

### Should you take Vyvanse the morning after drinking?

This is a common question with no one-size-fits-all answer, which is exactly why it belongs with your prescriber. Some general points:

- **Don't take an extra dose to push through.** More stimulant on top of dehydration, little sleep, and a stressed heart is the wrong direction.
- **Don't change your routine on your own.** Whether to take your usual dose, delay it, or skip a day is a decision to make with your doctor ahead of time, not on a hungover morning.
- **Be honest with yourself about how you feel.** If your heart is racing, you're shaky, or you feel unwell, that's a reason to call your doctor or pharmacist before taking anything.

### Getting through the next day

The basics are the same as any hangover, with a couple of Vyvanse-specific additions:

- **Drink water steadily** through the morning. An electrolyte drink can help if you're very dried out.
- **Eat, even if you're not hungry.** If you took your dose, your appetite may be low again, so plan simple food you'll actually eat.
- **Rest if you can.** Sleep debt is a big part of why this hangover hurts.
- **Go easy on caffeine.** Coffee on top of a stimulant and a rattled heart can make jitteriness and palpitations worse.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one for a headache, read the label and don't stack products. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers how to use acetaminophen safely after drinking.

If sleep is the main problem, our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) has practical tips that apply here too.

## How Long After Vyvanse Can You Drink?

There is no official, universal waiting period, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours that applies to everyone is guessing. Here is what you can say with confidence:

- **The effects usually last about 10 to 14 hours,** and the drug takes longer than that to fully leave your body. Even when you no longer feel it, some active drug is still circulating.
- **A morning dose is often still active in the early evening.** If you take it at 8 a.m. and start drinking at 6 p.m., you are almost certainly drinking while it's working.
- **Timing doesn't remove the risk, it lowers it.** Drinking late at night after the effects have faded is less risky than drinking in the middle of the active window, but the heart, sleep, and mood effects can still overlap.
- **The safest plan is one you've made with your prescriber.** Some doctors are fine with an occasional light drink well after the dose has worn off. Others will advise avoiding alcohol entirely, depending on your health, dose, and history.

What you should **not** do is skip your dose for a day so you can drink, or take your dose later than usual and then drink, without first checking with your doctor. Changing timing can affect your sleep and your symptoms, and it's the kind of adjustment your prescriber should weigh in on.

## Does Alcohol Make Vyvanse Less Effective?

Alcohol doesn't stop Vyvanse from being converted into its active form, and there's no good evidence that a drink changes how the capsule releases the drug. Because Vyvanse is a prodrug rather than a coated extended-release bead, it doesn't have the "dose dumping" concern that comes up with some other long-acting medicines when they're taken with alcohol.

But in a practical sense, alcohol works against what Vyvanse is trying to do:

- **ADHD symptoms get worse.** Alcohol lowers inhibition and impairs focus, working memory, and impulse control, which are the very things the medication is supposed to help.
- **Your sleep suffers,** and poor sleep makes ADHD symptoms worse the next day.
- **The next day is harder to manage,** so the medication may seem to "work less" when the real problem is the hangover and lost sleep.

So while alcohol doesn't chemically cancel the drug, regular drinking can make your treatment feel less effective overall.

## Vyvanse vs. Adderall With Alcohol: Is One Safer?

Vyvanse and Adderall are close cousins. Both are amphetamines, and the active drug from Vyvanse (dextroamphetamine) is also one of the ingredients in Adderall. The core risks with alcohol are the same: masking, heart strain, dehydration, and a rough next day. Neither one is "safe to drink on."

The differences come down to timing and shape of the effect:

| | Vyvanse | Adderall IR | Adderall XR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active drug | Dextroamphetamine (released from a prodrug) | Mixed amphetamine salts | Mixed amphetamine salts |
| Typical duration | About 10 to 14 hours | About 4 to 6 hours | About 10 to 12 hours |
| Onset | Gradual | Fast | Fast, then a second release |
| Likely to overlap with evening drinking | Very likely | Less likely for a morning dose | Likely |

The practical takeaway: because Vyvanse lasts so long, an evening drink is more likely to overlap with active medication than it would be with a single morning dose of immediate-release Adderall. For a fuller look at the Adderall side, see our guide to [Adderall and alcohol](/never-hungover/adderall-and-alcohol).

## Other Medications and Substances to Watch

Vyvanse's prescribing information lists several interactions. A few are especially relevant on a night out:

- **Antidepressants and other serotonin-affecting drugs.** Amphetamines combined with certain antidepressants (such as SSRIs, SNRIs, and MAO inhibitors), some migraine medicines, and other serotonin-raising drugs can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, a rare but serious reaction. MAO inhibitors must not be taken with Vyvanse at all. If you take any antidepressant, ask your prescriber how alcohol fits in.
- **Things that change urine acidity.** Amphetamines are cleared through the urine, and how acidic or alkaline the urine is changes how fast they leave the body. Large amounts of antacids or certain other alkalinizing agents can make amphetamine stay around longer. Mention any regular antacid use to your pharmacist.
- **Caffeine and energy drinks.** These add more stimulation to your heart and nervous system. Mixing energy drinks with alcohol is already linked with more drinking and more risk-taking. Doing it on Vyvanse adds a third stimulant layer.
- **Other drugs.** Cocaine, MDMA, and other recreational stimulants carry serious heart risks on their own and are particularly dangerous on top of Vyvanse and alcohol.

For a broader look at how common medicines and supplements interact with alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining Vyvanse and alcohol if you:

- Have a **heart condition**, high blood pressure, a heart rhythm problem, or a family history of sudden cardiac death
- Have **anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder**, or a history of psychosis
- Have had **seizures**
- Take **antidepressants** or other medicines that affect serotonin
- Are on a **higher dose** or recently had your dose increased
- Tend to **binge drink** or have trouble stopping once you start
- Barely eat during the day while on the medication

If any of these apply, have a short, honest conversation with your prescriber. They've heard this question many times, and it's much better to plan ahead than to find out the hard way.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

> **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you or someone else has:**
> - Chest pain or tightness
> - A pounding, very fast, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle after resting
> - Fainting, or feeling like you're about to pass out
> - Trouble breathing
> - Severe confusion, agitation, paranoia, or hallucinations
> - A seizure
> - A very high body temperature, heavy sweating, muscle stiffness, or shaking (possible overheating or serotonin syndrome)
> - Signs of alcohol poisoning: vomiting while barely conscious, slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, or being impossible to wake

Don't let someone "sleep it off" if they have signs of alcohol poisoning. Turn them on their side and get help. Because the stimulant can mask how drunk someone is, a person can look more alert than their blood alcohol level suggests right up until they don't.

**Call your doctor soon (not an emergency) if:**

- You regularly feel your heart race or skip after drinking on Vyvanse
- Your mood dips badly the day after drinking, or you have thoughts of harming yourself (if those thoughts feel urgent, call or text 988 in the US)
- You're finding it hard to sleep most nights
- You're unsure whether to take your dose after a night out

## A Practical Plan If You Do Drink

If you and your prescriber have agreed that an occasional drink is OK for you, here's how to keep the risk as low as possible:

1. **Plan the timing.** Drink later, well after your dose has peaked, rather than in the afternoon or early evening.
2. **Eat a full meal first.** Vyvanse may have hidden your hunger all day. Eat anyway.
3. **Set a number and count.** Decide on one or two drinks before you start. Don't go by how drunk you feel, because Vyvanse is lying to you about that.
4. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water for every drink.
5. **Skip energy drinks and shots.** No caffeinated mixers, and avoid fast drinking.
6. **Don't drive.** Feeling sharp is not the same as being sober.
7. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed and give yourself time to rest the next morning.

Most of the habits in our [how to prevent a hangover guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) apply here too, and they matter even more when you're on a stimulant.

## Where DHM Fits (And Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that some people take around drinking. It has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts on the brain. Most of that research is from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. It's interesting, not proven.

Here's what's important for anyone on Vyvanse:

- **DHM does not make it safe to drink on Vyvanse.** There is no good evidence that it reduces the masking effect, protects your heart, or changes how the two drugs interact.
- **There's little research on DHM combined with stimulant medications.** Check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement to a prescription, including this one.
- **It isn't a substitute for drinking less.** The best way to soften a "Vyvanse hangover" is fewer drinks, more water, real food, and enough sleep.

If you've cleared it with your doctor and want to try DHM on nights you do have a drink, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Vyvanse and alcohol don't cause a dramatic chemical reaction, but the combination is risky because the stimulant hides how drunk you are.
- Both drugs strain your heart, both dehydrate you, and together they wreck sleep and mood, which is why the "Vyvanse hangover" feels so bad.
- Vyvanse lasts around 10 to 14 hours, so evening drinks often overlap with active medication.
- Talk to your prescriber before combining them. If you do drink, keep it to one or two, count deliberately, eat first, drink water, and never drive.
- Chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, fainting, confusion, or a seizure means calling 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol on Vyvanse?**

Most prescribers recommend avoiding alcohol or keeping it very light while on Vyvanse. The two don't have a dramatic chemical reaction, but Vyvanse masks how drunk you feel, which makes overdrinking easy, and both put extra strain on your heart. Talk to your prescriber before combining them. If you do drink, keep it to one or two drinks, eat first, and count your drinks instead of going by how you feel.

**How long after taking Vyvanse can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Vyvanse's effects usually last about 10 to 14 hours, so a morning dose is often still active in the early evening. Drinking later, after the effects have worn off, lowers the overlap but doesn't remove every risk. Ask your prescriber what's reasonable for your dose and health, and don't skip or shift doses to make room for drinking without checking first.

**What is a Vyvanse hangover?**

People use the term for the rough morning after drinking on Vyvanse. It's usually worse than a normal hangover because the stimulant masking leads to more drinking, the medication and alcohol together disrupt sleep, low appetite leaves you dehydrated and under-fed, and the stimulant comedown adds fatigue and low mood. Water, food, rest, and going easy on caffeine help. If your heart is racing or you feel unwell, call your doctor or pharmacist.

**Is it dangerous to mix Vyvanse and alcohol?**

It can be. For a healthy adult on a normal dose who has one drink, a serious problem is unlikely. The danger rises with heavier drinking, higher doses, heart conditions, dehydration, and other medications such as antidepressants. The biggest practical risks are drinking far more than you realize, heart rhythm problems, and impaired judgment while feeling alert. Chest pain, fainting, or an irregular heartbeat that won't settle needs emergency care.

**Does alcohol cancel out Vyvanse?**

No. Alcohol doesn't stop Vyvanse from being converted to its active form, and there's no good evidence it changes how the capsule releases the drug. But alcohol works against the medication's goals by impairing focus and impulse control and disrupting sleep, so regular drinking can make your ADHD treatment feel less effective.

**Is Vyvanse safer than Adderall with alcohol?**

Not really. Both are amphetamines and carry the same core risks with alcohol: masking, heart strain, dehydration, and a harder next day. Vyvanse lasts longer than immediate-release Adderall, so evening drinks are more likely to overlap with active medication. Neither one is safe to drink on without talking to your prescriber.

**Should I take my Vyvanse the morning after drinking?**

That's a question to settle with your prescriber ahead of time, not on a hungover morning. Don't take an extra dose to push through, and don't change your routine on your own. If your heart is racing, you feel shaky, or you're very unwell, call your doctor or pharmacist before taking your dose.

**Can DHM help if I drink on Vyvanse?**

There's no good evidence that DHM reduces the risks of combining Vyvanse and alcohol, and it doesn't make the combination safe. Research on DHM is mostly from animal and lab studies, and there's little data on using it alongside stimulant medication. Check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement to a prescription.
